summary:
Siirt province stands under the national framework of Turkey, and every visitor-facing rule bearing on a trans traveller in the province comes from that layer. Siirt has no separate legal regime of its own on this question: the inventory contains no Siirt-specific ban, enforcement programme, incident or local institution concerning transgender visitors.

Both sources treat Siirt only as an instance of the national framework, and neither records an assembly ban, an identity stop, a detention or a prosecution inside the province's boundaries. A trans visitor should expect the country-wide assessment recorded at Turkey's national level to apply in Siirt without provincial variation, and should not expect any local safeguard or documentation practice specific to the province.
tangentialFactors:
The authority that produces the documented exposure elsewhere in Turkey rests in Siirt with the provincial governor and the provincial police directorate, the same offices that hold the power to ban public assemblies and to conduct street identity checks anywhere in the country. The inventory records no occasion on which either power has been used against a trans person or an LGBT gathering inside Siirt.

Neither source examines Siirt in its own right. The province's silence in both reports reflects the scope of their coverage as much as conditions on the ground, and a jurisdiction that appears in no count of incidents is not thereby shown to be free of them.
localsOnly: No resident-facing fact specific to Siirt is sourced. The inventory holds nothing on how trans residents of Siirt obtain or renew identity documents, which local office handles a gender-marker change, whether any facility in the province dispenses hormone therapy privately, or whether any local organisation exists to support LGBT residents. Neither source contains a Siirt entry, so conditions for trans residents here are described only through the country-wide framework.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Siirt's governor has issued any order restricting assembly or public expression on family or moral grounds is unresolved. No such order for Siirt appears in the inventory, and the two sources do not survey every province, so silence here is not evidence of permission.

Whether an incident involving a trans person has occurred in Siirt and gone unrecorded is unresolved. The negative finding rests on Amnesty International's Türkiye country report and an encyclopaedic survey of LGBT rights in Turkey, neither of which carries a Siirt entry.

Questions about the national legislative packages described in those sources, including whether they were ever submitted to parliament, sit outside this province's scope and are carried at Turkey's national level. The same applies to the status of criminalisation, legal gender recognition, marriage recognition and military service rules.

Local verification is absent: nothing in the inventory shows how Siirt police would act on a gender-marker mismatch during an identity check, whether a detained trans visitor would be held in the province or moved elsewhere, or which facility would receive them.
